1254.title: The grave
1254.howItsDone: Muslims visit graves to remember the hereafter, greet the dead with salam, and ask forgiveness for them; the time between death and the Day of Resurrection is called the barzakh, or the life of the grave.

segments.voice: Yesterday: mawt, death, and the soul at peace called back to its Lord.

Two seas, loosed by their Lord, run up against each other and meet. Water against water. The Qur'an, in Surah ar-Rahman, says of them, in Pickthall's words: "There is a barrier between them. They encroach not." The Arabic for that barrier is barzakh. Hold on to it, because the same word turns up somewhere much quieter. Not at the shoreline. At the graveside.
screen: `TWO SEAS, SIDE BY SIDE.` → `A BARRIER BETWEEN THEM.` → `THE SAME WORD, AT THE GRAVE.`

segments.voice: In Surah al-Mu'minun, someone at the point of death begs to be sent back, to do the good they left undone. The answer is no, and then a phrase, Pickthall again: "and behind them is a barrier until the day when they are raised." Barzakh. So the word that holds two seas apart also names the stretch between dying and rising: not this world any more, not yet the Day. The in-between. It's also spoken of as the grave, al-qabr, though the barzakh is more than a hole in the ground. What happens there? The Qur'an says little in detail, and the hadith say more. One in Sahih al-Bukhari, narrated by Ibn 'Umar, says that when a person dies, their place in the next life is shown to them morning and evening, and they are told: this is your place, until Allah raises you. So the in-between is not empty waiting. It is waiting with a view. Since it's part of the unseen, al-ghayb, scholars are careful to say the hadith describe it without explaining how. And notice what this does to a graveyard. A hadith in Sahih Muslim has the Prophet, peace be upon him, going out at night to the graveyard of al-Baqi' in Medina, greeting the dead with peace and asking forgiveness for them. He greets them because, in this teaching, the people in those graves are not gone. They are across a barrier: like the two seas, close, side by side, and kept apart.
screen: `SEND ME BACK. THE ANSWER IS NO.` · `A BARRIER UNTIL THE DAY OF RAISING.` · `WAITING, WITH A VIEW.` · then, large: `GREETING THE ONES ACROSS THE BARRIER.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one person who has died, someone you knew or someone whose name you only heard, and think of them not as gone but as across a barrier. If you pray, greet them as the Prophet greeted the dead at al-Baqi', with peace, and ask forgiveness for them; if not, say their name once and wish them well. And if missing someone is too heavy to carry alone, in the US call or text 988, any hour; elsewhere, local emergency help.
Barzakh. A barrier; in Muslim teaching, the in-between of the grave, from death until the Day of rising. Today's word.
Your line: the in-between. Close, side by side, and kept apart, like the two seas. Back tomorrow, same hill.

1255.title: The questions
1255.hook: three questions in the grave: who is your Lord, what is your religion, who is this man
1255.howItsDone: Muslims teach the three questions of the grave to children, and at burials those present may pray for the deceased to be made firm when the angels question them.

segments.voice: Yesterday: barzakh, the in-between, where the dead are close to us and kept apart.

Who is your Lord? What is your religion? Who is this man who was sent among you? Three questions. No multiple choice, no notes, no time to look anything up. In the hadith that tell of the grave, two angels ask them, soon after the mourners have walked away. One hadith in Sahih al-Bukhari even says the dead person hears the footsteps of the people leaving. Then the questions begin.
screen: `THREE QUESTIONS.` → `NO NOTES, NO LOOKING IT UP.` → `THE FOOTSTEPS WALK AWAY.`

segments.voice: The long hadith of al-Bara' ibn 'Azib, collected by Abu Dawud, lays it out. Two angels come and sit the person up. Who is your Lord? The believer says: my Lord is Allah. What is your religion? My religion is Islam. Who is this man who was sent among you? He is the Messenger of Allah. A hadith in Tirmidhi gives the two angels names: Munkar and Nakir. Then the other side of the scene. The one who lived without faith is asked the same three questions, and the answer, in paraphrase, is: I don't know. I heard people saying something, so I said it. That's the whole failure. Not a wrong theory. A borrowed answer, repeated without ever being one's own. The Qur'an has a verse that a hadith in Bukhari ties to this moment, in Pickthall's words: "Allah confirmeth those who believe by a firm saying in the life of the world and in the Hereafter." The answer holds in the grave because it was held in life. Some teachers draw a plain lesson from it. You can't memorize your way through these questions the night before, because they aren't testing memory. They ask what you actually lived by. Who did you turn to when it counted? What way did you follow on an ordinary day? Whose example did you keep? That's today's line: answer now. The exam is set in advance, and every day is a chance to work on the answers.
screen: `TWO ANGELS SIT THE PERSON UP.` · `MY LORD IS ALLAH.` · `I HEARD PEOPLE SAYING SOMETHING.` · then, large: `A FIRM SAYING, HELD IN LIFE.`

segments.voice: Take the three questions slowly, in your own words: who or what did I actually turn to this week when things went wrong; what way do I live by when no one is watching; whose example am I following? If you're Muslim, you may want to say the answers the hadith gives, and ask whether this week said them too; if you're not, let your honest answers be what they are, without judging them.

1256.title: The trumpet
1256.hook: the trumpet is blown, and all rise (39:68)
1256.howItsDone: Muslims believe the trumpet will be blown at the end of the world and again at the resurrection; the verses that describe it are recited in prayer and in sermons about the Last Day.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the questions of the grave, and your line, answer now: an answer held in life holds in the grave.

Some sounds end things. A final whistle. A school bell at three. An alarm at six that ends the night whether you're ready or not. The Qur'an speaks of one sound that ends everything, and then starts it again. In Surah az-Zumar, Pickthall's translation reads: "And the trumpet is blown, and all who are in the heavens and all who are in the earth swoon away, save him whom Allah willeth. Then it is blown a second time, and behold them standing waiting!" Two blasts. One to end, one to raise.
screen: `SOUNDS THAT END THINGS.` → `ONE BLAST TO END.` → `ONE BLAST TO RAISE.`

segments.voice: You heard the trumpet in An-Naba' on day 221; today, both blasts. The Arabic is as-sur, a horn. It sounds in more than one surah, in az-Zumar and again in Ya Sin, in a short, sudden line: and the trumpet is blown. Tradition names the angel who blows it Israfil, though the Qur'an itself doesn't give the name. The first blast brings a swoon over everyone in the heavens and the earth, except whoever Allah wills. Who those exceptions are, the verse leaves open, and commentators have answered in different ways. Then the second blast, and people stand, waiting. How long between the two? A hadith in Sahih al-Bukhari, narrated by Abu Hurayrah, says: between the two blasts is forty. Someone asks him: forty days? He declines to say. Forty months? He declines. Forty years? He declines again. A companion of the Prophet, peace be upon him, who would not go past what he had said, and readers take that restraint as part of the teaching. Then Ya Sin gives the moment of waking. When the trumpet is blown, people hurry from their graves to their Lord, and their first words, Pickthall again, are: "Woe upon us! Who hath raised us from our place of sleep?" The grave, from the far side, felt like sleep. The answer comes straight back: this is what the Beneficent promised, and the messengers told the truth. So in Muslim teaching the trumpet is not only an ending. It's the sound that means nobody was lost.
screen: `AS-SUR: A HORN, BLOWN TWICE.` · `THE SWOON, SAVE WHOM ALLAH WILLS.` · `FORTY WHAT? HE DECLINED TO SAY.` · then, large: `WHO HATH RAISED US FROM OUR SLEEP?`

segments.voice: Sit low, or lie down, and let your body go heavy, as if you'd been asleep a long time, with the line from Ya Sin in mind: who hath raised us from our place of sleep? Near the end, rise slowly, feet taking your weight, spine lifting, head coming up last; if standing is hard, simply lift your head. Stand still for a few breaths, with the verse from az-Zumar if you pray, or just noticing what it feels like to get up.

1257.title: The gathering
1257.hook: all people gathered on one plain
1257.howItsDone: Muslims believe all people will be raised and gathered for judgment on the Day of Resurrection; teachers sometimes point to the crowds of the Hajj at Arafat, all in plain white, as a reminder of that gathering.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the trumpet, blown twice, and your line: all will rise. Nobody lost.

No skyline. No street signs. No tree to meet under, no house to point at, no hill to climb for a better view. A hadith in Sahih al-Bukhari describes the ground of the Day of Resurrection like that: a white land, tinged with red, like a round loaf of fine flour, with no landmark on it belonging to anyone. Flat, open, and nobody's property. On that plain, the Qur'an says, every person will stand.
screen: `NO SKYLINE, NO SIGNS.` → `A LAND LIKE A LOAF OF FINE FLOUR.` → `NO LANDMARK FOR ANYONE.`

segments.voice: The Arabic is al-hashr, the gathering, and the Day is sometimes called yawm al-hashr. Surah al-Kahf says Allah will gather them and leave not one of them behind. Not one. And notice what's missing on that plain. In this life people gather by something: a city, a team, a language, a family name, a mosque, a church. Here, the hadith says, there's no landmark for anyone. No one's corner, no one's side of town. The Qur'an adds that each will come alone, as they were first created. Another hadith in Bukhari makes it even plainer. The Prophet, peace be upon him, said people will be gathered barefoot, unclothed, as they were born. 'A'ishah, his wife, heard it and asked the obvious question: men and women, looking at one another? And he answered, in paraphrase: the matter will be too serious for them to care about that. Everything people usually notice about each other, clothes, status, looks, is gone, and so is the urge to notice it. What's left is a person, and what they did. So the gathering is two things at once: a crowd with no one missing, all together on one plain, and each person in it standing alone, coming as they were made. The next days of this part follow what happens on that plain.

segments.voice: Picture a wide, flat, pale plain, and set on it the people closest to you, then the people you saw today, the stranger in line, the neighbor, then people from far away and from history, even people you've argued with, until it's full, with no landmarks and no sides. Stand among them and notice that nothing marks you out. If you pray, you can ask for mercy for all of them, in whatever words your tradition uses; if not, simply look at the crowd with kindness.

1258.title: The book in hand
1258.howItsDone: Muslims believe angels record each person's deeds and that the record will be given to them on the Day of Resurrection, in the right hand or the left; the hope to receive it in the right hand appears in prayers and sermons.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the gathering, everyone on one plain, with not one left behind.

A kid bursts out of the school gate on the last day of school, waving a report card over their head. Look! Read it! They can't wait for someone to see. The Qur'an has a moment with that same joy in it, on the Day of Resurrection. In Surah al-Haqqah, Pickthall's translation reads: "Then, as for him who is given his record in his right hand, he will say: Take, read my book!"
screen: `A REPORT CARD, WAVED HIGH.` → `GIVEN IN THE RIGHT HAND.` → `TAKE, READ MY BOOK!`

segments.voice: The Qur'an speaks of a written record of each life, kitab, a book. Surah al-Infitar speaks of guardians, noble recorders, who know what people do. On the Day, the book is handed over. In the right hand, joy: take, read my book. In al-Haqqah the next scene is the opposite. The one handed the book in the left hand says, in paraphrase: I wish I had never been given my book, I wish I had never known my reckoning. Same plain, same book, two faces. And who reads it? Surah al-Isra' answers, Pickthall again: "Read thy book. Thy soul sufficeth as reckoner against thee this day." You read your own. Surah al-Kahf adds that those who see their books ask what kind of book this is, which leaves nothing out, small or great. Small things: a tone of voice, a held door. If that were the whole picture it would be frightening, and here a hadith in Sahih al-Bukhari changes the arithmetic. The Prophet, peace be upon him, said that Allah wrote down good deeds and bad ones. Whoever intends a good deed and doesn't do it, one full good deed is written for them. If they do it, ten, up to seven hundred times, or more. Whoever intends a bad deed and holds back, that's written as a good deed; if they do it, it's written as one. The book counts everything, and it counts generously. So it's a record, not a trap: there is still time to write in it.
screen: `KITAB: A WRITTEN RECORD OF EACH LIFE.` · `RIGHT HAND, LEFT HAND.` · `READ THY BOOK.` · then, large: `IT COUNTS EVERYTHING, AND GENEROUSLY.`

segments.voice: Find one good thing you've been meaning to do and haven't, small is fine, a visit you keep putting off, returning something you borrowed, and hold the intention clearly, because by the hadith the intention alone is already written. Then picture yourself doing it, in a particular place, at a particular time. If you pray, you can ask that it be accepted.

1259.title: The scale
1259.hook: deeds weighed, and good character the heaviest (Tirmidhi)
1259.howItsDone: Muslims believe deeds will be weighed on the mizan on the Day of Resurrection, and teachers cite the hadith that nothing is heavier on it than good character; the two phrases 'light on the tongue, heavy on the scale' are part of daily remembrance.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the book in hand, a record that counts everything, and counts generously.

Some companions of the Prophet, peace be upon him, once laughed at Abdullah ibn Mas'ud. He had climbed a tree, the wind caught his clothes, and his legs showed, thin as sticks. A report in the Musnad of Ahmad says the Prophet asked what they were laughing at, and they said: his thin shins. And he answered that those legs would be heavier on the scale than the mountain of Uhud. Same legs. A different scale.
screen: `THIN LEGS, AND LAUGHTER.` → `HEAVIER THAN A MOUNTAIN.` → `A DIFFERENT SCALE.`

segments.voice: The word is mizan, a balance, a pair of scales. The Qur'an speaks of a just balance set up on the Day of Resurrection, so that no soul is wronged, and says even the weight of a mustard seed will be brought. Surah al-Qari'ah puts it in two lines: the one whose scales are heavy will have a pleasing life; the one whose scales are light, an abyss. So what is heavy? Jami' at-Tirmidhi records the Prophet saying, in paraphrase, that nothing is heavier on the believer's scale on the Day of Resurrection than good character, and that Allah dislikes the one who is foul and coarse in speech. Not the longest night prayer. Not the largest gift. Good character. Another hadith in the same collection says that by good character a person reaches the rank of one who fasts and prays. Arabic has a word for it, husn al-khuluq, beauty of character: patience in traffic, gentleness with a slow parent, honesty when nobody would know. And Sahih al-Bukhari closes with a hadith about two phrases, light on the tongue, heavy on the scale, beloved to the Most Merciful: subhan Allah wa bihamdihi, subhan Allah al-'azim. Glory be to Allah and His is the praise; glory be to Allah, the Mighty. Put together, the scale works the opposite way from the world. The world weighs size, money, looks, the legs in the tree. The mizan, in these texts, weighs a soft answer and a remembered God.

segments.voice: Bring to mind someone whose good nature made a hard moment lighter, and stay with them for a few breaths. Then see the moment ahead where you're most likely to be short with someone, a long line, a child at bedtime, and see yourself meeting it gently, with a slower answer and one kind sentence. If you pray, say the two light phrases, subhan Allah wa bihamdihi, subhan Allah al-'azim; if not, rest on the word gentle.
Mizan. The balance on which deeds are weighed on the Day; in a hadith in Tirmidhi, nothing on it is heavier than good character. Today's word.
Your line: character is heavy. Thin legs, and a heavy scale on the Day. See you tomorrow.

1260.title: The bridge
1260.hook: a bridge over the fire, crossed by light
1260.howItsDone: Muslims ask for the straight path in al-Fatiha when they pray, and teach from the hadith that on the Day of Resurrection people will cross a bridge, the sirat, over the fire, by the light of their deeds.

segments.voice: Yesterday: mizan, the scale, and your line: character is heavy. Nothing weighs more on it than good character.

Show us the straight path. Muslims say that line, from al-Fatiha, in their daily prayers; in Pickthall's translation it is simply "Show us the straight path." The Arabic for path there is sirat. In the hadith about the Day of Resurrection, sirat names a path no one walks lightly: a bridge, laid over the fire, that people must cross. One word, then, for a path asked for in prayer and for a crossing made once.
screen: `SHOW US THE STRAIGHT PATH.` → `SIRAT: THE PATH.` → `A BRIDGE OVER THE FIRE.`

segments.voice: A long hadith in Sahih al-Bukhari, narrated by Abu Sa'id al-Khudri, describes it. A bridge is set over Hell, slippery, with hooks along it. People cross at very different speeds. Some go over like the blink of an eye. Some like lightning, some like the wind, some like fast horses or riding camels. Some come through safe, some come through scratched, and some fall. In Sahih Muslim, Abu Sa'id adds something he says had reached him: that the bridge is thinner than a hair and sharper than a sword. He's careful to say it reached him. Another hadith in Bukhari, from Abu Hurayrah, says that on that day only the messengers will speak, and what they say is, in paraphrase: O Allah, keep safe, keep safe. Even the prophets, praying for the crossing. So how does anyone get across? In Surah al-Hadid, Pickthall: on the day when the believers are seen, men and women, "their light shining forth before them and on their right hands." They cross by light. The next verse has the hypocrites calling out to borrow some of that light, and being turned back. Light can't be borrowed on the Day. It has to be brought. Where does it come from? A hadith in Sahih Muslim gives one answer: prayer is light, charity is proof, patience is brightness. So some teachers join the two sirats. The straight path asked for in every prayer is practice for the bridge: walk it here by the light of what you do, and that light walks with you there.
screen: `A BRIDGE OVER THE FIRE.` · `BLINK, LIGHTNING, WIND, HORSES.` · `KEEP SAFE, KEEP SAFE.` · then, large: `LIGHT BEFORE THEM, AND ON THEIR RIGHT.`

segments.voice: The hadith named three sources of light: prayer, charity, patience. Choose one, perhaps one prayer said slowly and on time if you pray, or a small gift given without fuss, or patience with one person who usually wears you down. Then, with each out-breath, picture a little light gathering in front of you, enough to see a few steps ahead.
Sirat. The path; in the hadith, the bridge over the fire that all must cross on the Day, and the same word as the straight path of al-Fatiha. Today's word.
Your line: cross with light. It can't be borrowed on the Day; it has to be brought. I'll be here tomorrow.
